summary: During extravehicular activities (EVAs), astronauts must carefully control their movements because even small forces applied in microgravity can produce body rotation, linear drift, and separation from the work surface. In addition, space motion sickness, which commonly occurs during the early phase of spaceflight, may adversely affect task performance through nausea, vertigo, fatigue, cognitive impairment, and spatial disorientation. This article proposes the conceptual Active Attitude and Vestibular Stabilization Backpack (AAVSS) system. The system integrates wearable control moment gyroscopes (CMGs) to damp unintended rotations, a limited GN₂ propulsion system for safe positioning when necessary, and a vestibular–somatosensory feedback module to support spatial orientation. Its objectives are to provide astronauts with a stable and predictable working platform, reduce propellant consumption, and limit the operational effects of sensory mismatch associated with microgravity. However, the proposition that AAVSS could reduce space motion sickness has not yet been directly demonstrated; this component should therefore be treated as a research hypothesis requiring validation through controlled ground analogues and human spaceflight studies.
details: The Active Attitude and Vestibular Stabilization Backpack (AAVSS) is a conceptual human–machine system designed to enhance astronaut safety, physical stability, and operational performance during extravehicular activities (EVAs). In microgravity, even minor reaction forces generated when using tools or interacting with spacecraft structures can cause unintended body rotation, linear drift, and separation from the work surface, forcing astronauts to reserve one hand for restraint and increasing overall workload. Compounding this challenge, space motion sickness—caused by a mismatch among vestibular, visual, proprioceptive, and somatosensory inputs during early spaceflight—can induce nausea, vertigo, fatigue, cognitive impairment, and spatial disorientation. Building on the safety logic of NASA’s Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue (SAFER), AAVSS integrates three primary subsystems into a wearable backpack: a closed-loop array of multi-axis Control Moment Gyroscopes (CMGs) that damp small, repetitive rotations without consuming fuel; a backup cold-gas nitrogen (GN2) thruster layer that activates only when CMG capacity is exceeded or separation risk occurs; and an experimental vestibular–somatosensory feedback module that delivers low-cognitive-burden tactile cues (pressure or vibration) to provide consistent external orientation references, which remains a research hypothesis regarding space motion sickness mitigation. To preserve human control authority so the astronaut can override the system at any time, AAVSS operates across four modes—Passive Monitoring, Precision Stabilisation, Task-Support, and Safety and Recovery—and requires validation through a phased roadmap encompassing multibody dynamic modelling, human-in-the-loop virtual reality simulations, neutral-buoyancy and air-bearing tests, parabolic flights, and standardized neurovestibular assessments.
